passage:
At the community centre's after-school club, the game was “fort.” Everyone drifted toward Indu without being told. She listened first. “Dhruv has an idea,” she said, and the noise dropped. Dhruv, who rarely spoke, mumbled, “We could have a secret door.” “Yes! Who wants to make it?” said Indu, and three hands went up. She gave the door to Dhruv.

When Meenal grabbed the blanket, Indu said, “Let's take turns, two minutes each.” Nobody groaned. Even the little ones stayed in the game. Afterwards Meenal said, “Indu's fort is the best.” Indu shook her head. “It's everyone's fort.”

qa.q: What was Dhruv's idea?
qa.a: Dhruv's idea was a secret door.

qa.q: What did Indu want the group to feel when saying, “It's everyone's fort”?
qa.a: Indu wanted everyone to feel included and proud of the fort together, so no single child's idea or effort outshone the others.

qa.q: What choice did Indu make when Meenal grabbed the blanket?
qa.a: Indu suggested taking turns of two minutes each, and nobody groaned.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt when Indu said, “Dhruv has an idea”?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt nervous and pleased to be noticed, since a leader made room for a quiet voice.

grounding: A child whom others follow in games listens to ideas, shares turns and leads by warmth and fairness.

passage:
I'm Mohit, and I live on the first floor of Arohi's building. Every evening the colony children play in the car park, and every evening they follow Arohi without anyone deciding it. I watched for a week. When the twins argued about who bats first, Arohi flipped a coin and said, “Loser fields first, winner bowls last.” Nobody shouted. When little Chintu wanted to join, she made him the scorer so he'd be included. Nobody seemed afraid of her; they smiled when she came down the stairs.

I can't say what she was feeling, but she never raised her voice and looked as if she enjoyed it. Even I, who hate cricket, wanted to play.

qa.q: What job did Arohi give Chintu?
qa.a: Arohi made Chintu the scorer.

qa.q: What might have made the children smile when Arohi came down the stairs?
qa.a: They probably felt safe and happy with Arohi, since Arohi is fair and never raised a voice, so following felt like fun, not fear.

qa.q: What choice did Arohi make when the twins argued about who bats first?
qa.a: Arohi flipped a coin and set a fair rule: loser fields first, winner bowls last.

qa.q: How might Chintu feel, being made the scorer?
qa.a: Chintu probably felt included and important, since a small child was given a real job.

grounding: An observer describes a child whom others follow in play, who shares turns and leads by warmth and fairness.

passage:
I'm Omkar, and in our building I'm the one who organises cricket.
I don't shout. I just ask. Last Sunday, Ujjwal, who is small and usually fields, said, “Can I bat first for once?” Some big boys groaned. I said, “Okay, Ujjwal opens today, and I'll go last.”
He got out in the second over, but he was grinning.
When Kunal wanted different teams, I let everyone pick one player each. When two boys fought about a catch, I said, “Replay it.” They laughed and did.
Everyone comes back every Sunday. I think it's because everybody gets a turn. It makes me really happy when they all shout my name from the ground, even the little ones.

qa.q: Who did Omkar say would open last Sunday?
qa.a: Ujjwal opens today, Omkar said.

qa.q: How does Omkar feel when everyone shouts from the ground?
qa.a: Omkar feels really happy and warm, glad that everyone keeps coming back.

qa.q: What makes Omkar a good leader in the games?
qa.a: Omkar listens to ideas, shares turns fairly and solves fights calmly, leading by warmth rather than shouting.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt batting first?
qa.a: He was probably excited and proud, grinning even after getting out, because he finally got a turn.

grounding: A child describes leading neighbourhood cricket by listening, sharing turns and keeping everyone happy, leading by fairness not fear.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, recess, Tuesday.
I have been watching Amandeep during recess. The other children follow her into every game, not because she is loud, but because she listens.
Today, when they were choosing teams for dodgeball, Chinmay, who is new and shy, stood at the side. Amandeep picked him first. When the older girls wanted to change the rules halfway, she asked everyone, “Hands up if you want new rules?” and went with the majority, even though her team was losing.
When a boy cried after being hit, she stopped the game and sat with him.
I've asked Amandeep to help me run the Sports Day warm-up. I'll keep an eye that she also gets time just to play.

qa.q: Who did Amandeep pick first?
qa.a: She picked Chinmay first.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Amandeep picked him first?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and happy, welcomed into the game as the new, shy boy.

qa.q: Why does the teacher want to give Amandeep a role but also watch her?
qa.a: Amandeep leads fairly and kindly, so giving her a role builds on that, while making sure she still has time to be a child and play.

qa.q: How might the older girls see Amandeep's hand-vote?
qa.a: They may have respected it, since she let the group decide even when her own team was losing.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who leads games by listening, sharing and fairness, and whom others follow out of warmth, not fear.

passage:
Friday
Summer camp treasure hunt today! I was the leader of Team Parrot. Ma'am chose me because I'm good at maps, but I didn't want to be bossy.
Hemant kept saying, “Can I hold the map?” The first time I said wait. The second time I gave it to him, and I held the torch. He found the second clue before me!
When Riya and Tanvi fought over who read the clues, I made them take turns. When little Bunty got tired, we all walked slowly.
We didn't win. We came second. But everyone hugged at the end, and Hemant said I was the best leader. I felt warm all over.
Gopika

qa.q: Which team did Gopika lead?
qa.a: Gopika led Team Parrot.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel at the end of the hunt?
qa.a: Gopika felt warm and happy, especially when Hemant said Gopika was the best leader.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that made the team happy?
qa.a: Gopika shared the map, made people take turns and slowed down for Bunty, leading with fairness.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt holding the map?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and trusted, especially when he found the second clue.

grounding: A child writes about leading a treasure hunt by sharing turns and keeping everyone happy, leading by warmth and fairness.

passage:
After school in Sonapur village, the children always waited for Farida before starting a game. Today it was hide-and-seek around the haystacks.
"Who wants to seek first?" she asked. Three hands shot up. "Lavanya hasn't had a turn all week. Lavanya?" The smallest girl beamed.
When big Raju said the haystacks behind the cowshed should be out of bounds, Farida thought for a moment. "Good idea. The calf is tied there."
When Lavanya couldn't find anyone for ages, Farida let a cough slip on purpose so Lavanya would find her.
Nobody was scared of Farida. They just liked playing when she was there.

qa.q: Where did the children play hide-and-seek?
qa.a: Around the haystacks.

qa.q: Why did Farida let a cough slip on purpose?
qa.a: Farida felt caring and a little worried that Lavanya would feel upset or left out, so she let herself be found.

qa.q: What makes Farida a leader the others want to follow?
qa.a: She listens to ideas like Raju's, shares turns fairly and looks out for the smallest player.

qa.q: What is playing like for Lavanya when Farida is there?
qa.a: Lavanya feels included and happy, beaming when she finally gets a turn to seek 😊

grounding: Shows a child whom others follow in play because she listens, shares turns and keeps everyone happy rather than using fear.
